content: The study conducted by Sanchez et al. in 2013 in Brazil reported a tuberculosis (TB) prevalence of 8 cases per 1,374 individuals (equivalent to 6,040 per 100,000) before the implementation of active case finding (ACF). After ACF was introduced, the prevalence decreased to 8 cases per 954 individuals (equivalent to 2,900 per 100,000). Similarly, the study by Tsegaye Sahle et al. in 2019 in Ethiopia found a TB prevalence of 3 cases per 3,024 individuals (99 per 100,000) before ACF. Following the introduction of ACF, the prevalence increased to 10 cases per 2,551 individuals (392 per 100,000). Four observational studies, conducted in Zambia (Maggard et al., 2015), India (Mallick et al., 2017), Uganda (Karamaggi et al., 2018), and the USA (Degner et al., 2016), evaluated the impact of ACF interventions. These studies used an uncontrolled before-and-after design. One study compared two types of ACF rather than comparing ACF to standard case detection. Three of the studies included co-interventions in addition to ACF. Measures of uncertainty were not available for these studies. The studies highlighted methodological limitations, including the lack of adjustment for potential confounders, absence of a gold standard for assessing disease severity, and low event rates in some cases. High risk of bias was noted due to unaccounted confounding by temporal trends. Variability in the methods of ACF evaluation and differences in the direction of effect between studies contributed to inconsistency and indirectness in the findings. The WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis (TB) screening emphasize the importance of using prolonged cough (lasting two weeks or more) as a screening criterion for TB in the general population. However, the sensitivity and specificity of this approach vary widely across studies. False negatives (patients incorrectly classified as not having active TB) and false positives (patients incorrectly classified as having active TB) were reported, with significant implications for resource allocation and follow-up testing. Chest X-ray (CXR) screening for TB, whether based on any abnormality or findings suggestive of TB, was evaluated in multiple studies. Sensitivity and specificity varied across studies, with some heterogeneity explained by factors such as WHO region, TB prevalence in the study population, and smoking prevalence. False positives and false negatives were reported, with resource implications for follow-up testing. The studies also highlighted issues with the reference standard and flow/timing domains, with many studies scoring high risk of bias. Only a small proportion of studies had low risk of bias in these domains. Variability in study design, economic region, and TB prevalence among participants contributed to heterogeneity in the findings. Overall, the evidence underscores the challenges in implementing and evaluating TB screening strategies, particularly in resource-limited settings. The findings emphasize the need for robust study designs, standardized methodologies, and careful consideration of contextual factors to optimize TB case detection and management.
